hints: Every nonnegative integer is a sum of four squares, so a solution always exists.
Precompute which values are sums of two squares and store one pair for each such value.
For each n, test a first square and look up whether the remainder is a sum of two squares.
analogy: Build a lookup table for two-square piles, then split the target into two such piles.
correctness: Every pair table entry is a valid sum of two squares. The four-square theorem guarantees a decomposition of n into two pairs, so the search over a and the pair lookup finds a valid four-square representation.
complexity: O(N) pair-generation time and O(N) lookup space up to constant factors; each query takes O(sqrt(n)) time, where N is the largest input and sum of inputs is bounded.
algorithm: Let N be the maximum input. Build pair[x] for sums x=a^2+b^2<=N by looping a,b<=sqrt(N), storing one witness pair. For each n, loop a<=sqrt(n); if pair[n-a^2] exists, output a and that pair's two values followed by 0, giving four squares.
